data.title: LVMH touts ‘special bond’ with China amid ‘subdued’ sales backdrop
data.description:
French luxury giant LVMH Group kicked off a global open-house event showcasing its craftsmanship in Shanghai on Thursday, as the event’s founder Antoine Arnault hailed a “special bond” with Chinese customers at a launch event in Paris.
It came as the group faced pressure from sluggish demand in China and a backlash over a lawsuit against a local tea company.
At the launch event at the Samaritaine department store in central Paris for this year’s Les Journées Particulières, first initiated by Arnault in 2011, he mentioned the Shanghai event, which was the first among 71 venues across 13 countries to open to the public for the three-day event.
“For the first time since the event was created, several LVMH houses have come together in a single venue to share our savoir faire and its dialogue with Chinese culture,” said Arnault, who holds multiple roles within LVMH and is the son of its chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault. “Because we share a special bond with China and our Chinese customers.”
The exhibition in Shanghai will gather 15 brands from the group, including Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine, Tiffany and Bulgari. Visitors will get a behind-the-scenes look at how some of the group’s iconic products are made, such as Louis Vuitton’s Speedy P9 bag.
LVMH held an opening ceremony in Zhangyuan, a historic neighbourhood near Nanjing Xilu, on Thursday, featuring a Chinese calligraphy ceremony.
Four venues in China will participate in this year’s event: two in Shanghai and one each in Hong Kong and Ningxia.

The event came as the group announced disappointing numbers from China earlier this week in its third-quarter results: sales declined 5 per cent in Asia excluding Japan, caused mainly by a sharp macro-led deterioration in Chinese consumer sentiment, according to the group.
Louis Vuitton’s lawsuit against local brand Molly Tea further complicated the situation for the French luxury giant in the world’s second biggest luxury market.
The local tea chain was ordered by a Chinese court to pay 10.3 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in restitution in July over its use of a logo similar to the French brand’s four-petaled flower. The initial ruling, despite the appeal, sparked heated online debate and drew public sympathy for the Chinese company.
“[It’s] very difficult to size a precise impact, but it’s probably fair to say that it had a negative impact, at least at the beginning of the quarter,” said Cecile Cabanis, LVMH’s chief financial officer, during an earnings call on Monday.
“The news flow has not been particularly good in China in the summer, so this has really weighed on the feel-good factor and created a short-term subdued Chinese backdrop. We hope it will subside. We need to do more, but we have not stopped investing in China.”
Like in previous years, LVMH will participate in this year’s China International Import Expo, set for Shanghai early next month.

data.title: Hong Kong police arrest 2 men over HK$1.7 million Kowloon break-in spree
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested two men over their alleged involvement in at least six break-ins across Kowloon over the past three months, with total losses amounting to HK$1.7 million (US$216,629).
The pair – a 54-year-old mainland Chinese man and a 34-year-old Hong Kong resident – were arrested separately on Thursday in Sham Shui Po and Tsim Sha Tsui, respectively.
Police identified and located them following a break-in targeting four flats in a private residential building on Farm Road in Kowloon City, where more than HK$100,000 in cash and watches, as well as some credit cards, were stolen.
At a press briefing on Friday, Tsang Ka-chun, a senior inspector with the Kowloon City district crime squad, said police attached great importance to the case and were able to identify and locate the two suspects after reviewing surveillance camera footage.
Initial investigations showed that the pair generally targeted private residential homes with unlocked windows or doors, while the flats were unoccupied at night.
“The mainland man would break into the flats and steal valuables. He would subsequently hand over the stolen credit cards to the Hong Kong man, who used them to make online purchases totalling around HK$30,000,” Tsang said.
“After subsequent investigations, detectives also believe the duo are connected with at least five burglary cases that took place in Kowloon City and Cheung Sha Wan between July and October,” he added.
In those cases, about HK$1.6 million in cash, handbags and jewellery were stolen.
The mainlander was arrested for attempted burglary and illegal immigration, while the local man was arrested for handling stolen goods and obtaining property by deception.
During Thursday’s operation, officers seized cash, credit cards and valuables, as well as clothes and shoes believed to belong to the suspects.
The two men remained in police custody for questioning on Friday evening.
Tsang urged flat owners to remain vigilant and take simple precautions, such as locking windows and doors before leaving home, and to install surveillance cameras.
Under the Theft Ordinance, the maximum penalty upon conviction for burglary or handling stolen goods is 14 years’ imprisonment, while obtaining property by deception carries a maximum sentence of 10 years.
Hong Kong logged 344 burglary cases in the first half of 2026, down 22.7 per cent from 445 in the same period last year, according to police statistics.
Burglaries fell to a record low of 818 cases, a 33.1 per cent year-on-year drop, in 2025.

data.title: AI-powered drones to help detect hill fires during Chung Yeung Festival
data.description:
Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department will launch three new AI-assisted drone technologies to strengthen fire detection and its response to heightened risks during tomb-sweeping activities ahead of the Chung Yeung Festival on Sunday.
Wong Tak-fai, acting divisional officer for information and communications technology, said on Friday that the technology would improve the speed and accuracy of fire detection to help the department operate more efficiently.
“Artificial intelligence [AI] not only speeds up the processing of drone images but, more importantly, helps our staff continuously analyse large amounts of images from different drones across various locations to identify situations needing priority attention,” Wong said.
With the Chung Yeung Festival approaching, the department will strengthen manpower to monitor high-risk locations for fires and step up district patrols and public education efforts with the Civil Aid Service and other district organisations.
The department will also deploy 159 firefighters on Saturday across 12 locations in New Territories North, 10 spots in Kowloon and another six locations in New Territories South. On Sunday, an additional 166 firefighters will be deployed.
Hong Kong recorded 693 hill fires in 2025.
The department will also mobilise a newly bought remotely operated aerial surveillance system consisting of an off-road vehicle from mainland Chinese manufacturer Geely retrofitted with two drone docking systems and a generator.
The HK$1.2 million system will allow officers to survey hard-to-reach fire hazard areas. Its drones can conduct automated patrols within a 3km radius and be controlled remotely.

A real-time artificial intelligence video analysis platform will also be used to speed up the analysis of drone footage and images to generate timely alerts for fire hazards or drownings.
The system uses AI to accurately identify signs of smoke and people who may be drowning, reducing the need for staff to review drone surveillance footage.
“The new platform will be able to receive the footage in real time during a drone flight and then simultaneously run an artificial intelligence analysis,” Wong said.
Currently, footage analysis takes place after a flight ends, with officers manually transferring the files from an SD card in the drone to a computer.
The department will also have two high-payload drones equipped with water-bomb systems ready for deployment against remote hill fires. Each drone costs HK$500,000, including batteries.
These drones can carry weights up to 150kg and are equipped with an 80-litre water tank, allowing them to release water bombs where needed.
Wong said that in departmental tests, while it took firefighters one hour to carry rescue equipment 5km uphill, the large drone could do it in 10 minutes.
“The Fire Services Department is exploring the use of large drones in frontline operations, hoping to move from surveillance and observation to delivering firefighting equipment,” Wong said.
However, the acting divisional officer said artificial intelligence would in no way replace firefighters, as he stressed that all operational decisions would still be made by humans.

data.title: ASML eyes hybrid bonding, report finds, as Chinese firms adopt chip technique
data.description:
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML is expanding into next-generation hybrid bonding, a technique that creates dense electrical connections by directly joining chips or silicon wafers, according to a new report. Major Chinese companies are also adopting the technology to improve chip performance.
ASML submitted 27 patent families related to hybrid bonding tools between December 2022 and November 2024, according to a report published by semiconductor and AI supply chain research firm SemiAnalysis on Thursday. The number could be higher because of publication delays affecting recent filings, it said.
The filings suggest ASML is moving beyond lithography, a market it dominates, into back-end processes as demand for high-performance chips surges amid the global artificial intelligence boom.
The company had also begun developing the architecture for a hybrid bonder with Dutch technology firms Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG, according to SemiAnalysis, citing industry media reports.
“We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for hybrid bonding,” SemiAnalysis said. “These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.”
The company has not officially announced the extent of its progress on advanced packaging. But CEO Christophe Fouquet said during an April earnings call that the company was “continuing to look for opportunities to support our customers” in hybrid bonding.
ASML told the South China Morning Post by email on Friday that it would “continue to look in which directions [the] 3D integration industry will evolve and to see how this relates to ASML’s roadmap, and where ASML’s expertise can be of added value”.
Hybrid bonding allows ultra-high-density electrical connections and is widely viewed as one of the next major trends in chipmaking. Recent breakthroughs by China’s Huawei Technologies and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) involved using the technique to improve performance as United States-led export restrictions limit access to some advanced semiconductor equipment.


Under those restrictions, Huawei and CXMT cannot import ASML’s most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines.
Hybrid bonding can reduce the thermal resistance in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks by about 30 per cent, according to a September report by Guotai Haitong Securities, which cited Samsung data. Lower thermal resistance can help heat escape more easily, potentially reducing cooling requirements and the need for related investments.
Huawei disclosed new details this week about its flagship Kirin 9050 series, the first mass-produced chip to use its proprietary LogicFolding architecture developed under a framework it calls the Tau Scaling Law. The company said the design integrated more than 50 million hybrid bonds and increased overall transistor density by 53.5 per cent.
CXMT, meanwhile, announced last week that its latest “4F square” dynamic random-access memory architecture used hybrid bonding, which could allow it to increase wafer bit density without relying on advanced EUV lithography.
Despite the potential benefits of the technique, China remained heavily dependent on imported hybrid bonding equipment, particularly advanced machines, according to a separate report by Huaan Securities.
The report noted that domestic equipment manufacturers were stepping up research and development to narrow the gap, with Piotech and Xinhui Lianxin among the leading players.
Piotech’s hybrid bonding equipment generated 136 million yuan (US$20.3 million) in revenue in 2025, up 41.9 per cent from a year earlier, according to its annual report.
Nomura analysts said in a report last week that Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture could drive demand for bonding equipment, as well as Piotech’s mainstay thin-film deposition tools.

data.title: 3 arrested over missing fire-safety parts in 48 Hong Kong lifts, source says
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested a director and two registered lift engineers on suspicion of deception in connection with faulty replacement works on 48 lifts at two housing estates, the South China Morning Post has learned.
The latest suspected faults come just months after a fiasco involving lifts at a new hospital block, and experts said on Friday a thorough review of the regulatory process could be needed
A source said the three suspects were from Taizoom Elevator, which replaced nine lifts at Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong and 39 lifts at Pok Hong Estate in Sha Tin.
One of the suspects was a 79-year-old director and shareholder of Taizoom. The other two were registered lift engineers who examined the installations and signed safety certificates, aged 63 and 82, respectively.

The arrests came a day after the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department said its inspection, triggered by a complaint, found that Taizoom had installed fire-resistant doors without the required door frame components at the two estates.
The department said the contractor had submitted a fire-resisting rating certificate and claimed it had completed the works.
Suspecting fraud and false statements, the department reported the case to police.
The insider said officers raided the company’s office in Chai Wan, and the investigation had found that the outstanding components were “critical smoke control devices”.
“The registered contractor and the registered engineer responsible for inspecting the lifts allegedly concealed the construction defects intentionally and falsely reported to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department and the owners’ corporation that the works were completed in accordance with the contract,” the source said.
The case has been referred to the regional crime unit of New Territories South.
According to the department’s quarterly performance rating for lift contractors, Taizoom scored three out of five in service quality and had the same score in safety performance as other companies.
The arrests came two months after 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new 34-storey clinical block were deemed unfit for use.
Law Wing-chai, a registered lift engineer involved in the hospital project, was sentenced to 160 hours of community service last month after being convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates.

Professor Ho Wing-ip, an adjunct professor at Polytechnic University’s department of electrical and electronic engineering, said both incidents might have been the result of lapses in supervision and a thorough review could be needed.
“After the two incidents, the public’s trust in registered lift engineers seems to have been shaken a bit ... We still do not know if they are just the tip of an iceberg or extremely rare cases. The department has to look thoroughly into the sector and report to the public,” he said.
“If they are the tip of an iceberg, then it requires a review of the existing system and mechanism.”
A lift can only go into service after the director of electrical and mechanical services issues or renews the required permit.
Only registered lift contractors can undertake works, which should be examined by a registered lift engineer.
Ho said the door frame components were intended to prevent flames and smoke from seeping through gaps if a fire broke out.
Typically, door frame components were only visible from the top of the lift car, he explained, adding that the department might have to request registered lift engineers to inspect them and include photos as records in the examination report.
Ho noted that lifts underwent monthly maintenance and annual inspections, but given the number in the city, checking every concealed part each time was unrealistic.
According to official information from February, Hong Kong had 73,393 lifts.
Louis Szeto Ka-sing, past chairman of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers’ mechanical, marine, naval architecture and chemical division, said authorities should first check whether similar problems existed in other lifts.
He pointed out that the problem might not only involve the contractor, registered lift professionals and the department, but also the supplier of the lift components, logistics parties, workers and work supervisors.
Szeto said it was possible the stakeholders had failed to communicate properly and could not identify the risks in advance.
“We have to look into the incident,” he said. “Only training and communication can help resolve potential risks.”
The department said on Thursday that it had started a comprehensive review of the installation of new equipment and lift modernisation, inspection and maintenance works, site supervision system and systems under the Lifts and Escalators Ordinance.

data.title: China’s AI infrastructure boom fuels earnings surge for local chip firms
data.description:
Chinese chip and tech firms have flagged as much as six-fold growth in unaudited third-quarter profits, as huge demand for home-grown processors and artificial intelligence infrastructure filters through links in the supply chain amid the country’s push for self-reliance.
Shanghai-listed Yuanjie Semiconductor Technology expected its quarterly net profit to land between 403 million yuan and 453 million yuan, up 579 per cent to 660 per cent from a year earlier.
The maker of laser chips for optical communications said data-centre demand was driving shipments and helping maintain high margins.
Some public firms offered a glimpse of their financial performance in the first nine months of the year, ahead of final third-quarter results announcements.
Graphics processing unit (GPU) designer MetaX, listed in Shanghai but also pursuing a Hong Kong listing, turned a profit in the period thanks to increasing orders. It estimated a net profit of between 587 million yuan (US$88 million) and 717 million yuan, reversing a year-earlier loss, even excluding non-recurring gains.

Hygon Information, whose processors serve both general computing and AI workloads, projected revenue growth of 50 per cent to 64 per cent in the first nine months. It cited rising demand for high-end chips as customers increasingly choose domestic alternatives over foreign suppliers.
Storage giant Shenzhen Longsys Electronics said its net profit during the period could reach 14 billion to 14.9 billion yuan, roughly 20 times the figure for the previous year. It noted that price increases for DRAM and NAND flash storage had slowed in the third quarter, giving profits a smaller boost.
Memory prices could remain firm through 2027, according to a Morgan Stanley report on Sunday, which also warned that supply catching up or customers slowing their purchases could cool the boom even without weaker AI demand.
Optical module supplier Accelink Technologies forecast a nine-month net profit growth of 65 per cent to 82 per cent, citing both global AI capital spending and Chinese cloud providers’ continued investment in data centres as profit drivers.
Silicon wafer supplier Xian Eswin Material Technology said its production lines ran at full capacity in the first nine months, with sales volumes up about 43 per cent to 8.3 million wafers. Although its net profit of about 151 million yuan during the period was boosted by gains from investments in initial public offerings by its customers, it still expected a loss after excluding non-recurring items.
China’s AI buildout and efforts to replace imported processors are bringing more business to local chip designers. Research firm TrendForce projected in August that Chinese-designed chips would account for almost 90 per cent of the country’s high-end AI processor market this year.
The growth in chip production is also lifting materials suppliers. Hubei Feilihua Quartz Glass forecast nine-month net profit growth of 35 per cent to 56 per cent, citing stronger semiconductor demand and opportunities to replace imported products.
The research firm Bernstein said in a Tuesday report that quartz components used in chipmaking equipment were already well localised in China, with further growth increasingly tied to orders for domestic chipmaking equipment.

data.title: Inspections ordered at 8 more houses in One Stanley after rebar scandal
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have ordered the developer of the One Stanley luxury estate to inspect eight more houses – including one acquired by a Mongolian mining tycoon’s family – and the common area of a flat, in the wake of a scandal involving alleged substandard works at a building in the residential development.
The details of the inspection were announced in a sales brochure updated on Friday by K&K Property, the developer of the neighbourhood in southern Hong Kong, after a detached house, No 35, was alleged to be defective due to insufficient steel bars used in parts of the building.
The Buildings Department announced in early October that it would conduct random checks on buildings in the estate, after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said he had tasked the Development Bureau to closely monitor the investigation into the case.
According to the brochure, the department had spotted irregularities in the house, including the absence of wire mesh on the concrete cover of a ground-floor beam, as required by the approved plan, and deviations in the steel reinforcement of some slabs.
The department told the developer to inspect houses No 5, 8, 16, 17, 19, 32, 33 and 36, as well as the common area of a flat, Block 9.
According to a source familiar with the matter, buyers had signed provisional purchase agreements on three of the houses – No 5, 16 and 17 – but none had requested to terminate the contracts so far.
The South China Morning Post earlier reported that Tisara Holdings, whose director is Tselmuun Nyamtaishir, signed a provisional agreement in January to purchase the No 5 house.
Nyamtaishir is the president and CEO of Mongolyn Alt (MAK), a mineral conglomerate founded in 1993 by her father in Mongolia and is the largest coal exporter in the country.
She earlier told the SCMP that the block was intended to be used as the retirement residence of the group’s founders.
Land Registry records show house No 16 was sold to Supreme Harmony Limited at HK$116.8 million (US$14.9 million). The company, whose owner is a mainland Chinese national, signed the sale and purchase agreement in June this year.
House No 17 was sold for HK$118 million to an individual, who signed the document in August.
The Buildings Department declined on Friday to comment on further investigation details.
Speaking to the press on Thursday, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho also declined to provide more details about the case, saying the investigation into No 35 by the Buildings Department was still ongoing.

Asked why the department deemed it appropriate to issue an occupation permit for the house, Linn said some problems might remain hidden to authorities.
“Sometimes, when an occupation permit is issued, there may be hidden areas that were not visible at the time,” she said.
“We will definitely make the investigation results public, act in accordance with the law, and punish offenders according to law.”
The issue first came to light after online property news outlet WuChatProp said on October 2 that an on-site inspection of the house found insufficient steel bars were used in some parts of the building, and the amount in certain areas fell short of the approved structural plan by as much as 75 per cent.
The owner, who submitted a complaint to the department in January, had lamented the government’s inaction, according to the report.
The property is a four-bedroom, 3,000-square-foot (278 square metre) detached house, which the owner reportedly bought in 2024. The price stood at HK$115.8 million, according to a transaction list obtained by the SCMP.
The problem was discovered as Hong Kong was hit with a string of construction scandals, including issues with concrete samples from three public housing blocks under construction in Tung Chung, prompting further review and testing in September.
Earlier in August, 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block were deemed unfit for use. The widespread installation defects delayed the full commissioning of the Pok Fu Lam hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year.
City leader Lee declined to comment on individual cases but said he was concerned as to whether the professionals involved in the projects had discharged their duties properly, adding that such matters concerned professional standards and the quality and safety of the city’s construction works.
In response to the scandal at One Stanley, K Wise, a subsidiary of K&K Property, said it would offer a six-year structural warranty to One Stanley homeowners and would also arrange free independent inspections.
It also said the owner and the developer had agreed to jointly hire an independent surveyor to determine the circumstances, while no other consensus was reached.

data.title: Ex-father-in-law failed to repay HK$250,000 loan, Abby Choi murder trial hears
data.description:
The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung failed to repay a HK$250,000 loan from her partner’s father and asked for help in hiring lawyers after he was remanded in custody for allegedly killing the model three years ago, a court has heard.
Tam Chak-kwan, founder of the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian, testified in the High Court on Friday about his interactions with Kwong Kau in the year leading to the latter’s arrest for his suspected role in Choi’s murder in February 2023.
Kwong, 68, allegedly enlisted his two sons to help kill the 28-year-old influencer after she tried to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin that was registered in his name.
He is standing trial alongside his sons Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, Choi’s ex-husband.
The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month.
The court heard Tam’s family wealth increased significantly after he received part of the profits from selling his business to a Japanese company for HK$1 billion.
He told the court it was “a little bit of an achievement”, but Deputy Judge Brian Keith said he did not have to be unduly modest.
The former restaurant owner said his son, Chris Tam Fong-chun, had a very happy relationship with Choi even though they never registered their marriage. He and his wife, Yau Mei-fung, never took issue with the model being a divorcee with two children from her first marriage to Alex Kwong, the court heard.
He said he gave Choi a HK$41 million flat at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, where he used to live, and more than HK$80 million for investments. The court was told that he and his wife also bought her luxury gifts including handbags and jewellery.
Asked why he allowed his de facto daughter-in-law to handle finances, the elder Tam said Choi was more mature and organised than his son, whom he said was not serious about work when he was young. He added that the socialite was able to handle money well and make good investment decisions.

Wrapping up his testimony on Friday, Chris Tam said his father spent about HK$6 million to help him settle a HK$5 million gambling debt he incurred when he visited Macau with Choi and Anthony Kwong in August 2021.
The younger Tam said he believed the additional payments were gratuities, colloquially known as “tea money”, given to people with triad affiliations for stopping debt collectors from continuing to harass his family.
The elder Tam said he was approached by five “fierce” men on a day in early 2022, telling him Choi owed HK$5 million because of his son.
The elder Tam said he was shocked to later confirm with his son that he had borrowed money to gamble in Macau. He then approached Kwong Kau, who advised him to report the matter to police, the court heard.
The witness said that as he was frustrated by the progress of the police investigation, he asked Kwong Kau for help again.
Kwong Kau allegedly said he could resolve the matter through “people in the underworld”, but Tam insisted the matter should be settled using a law firm.
The elder Tam said he transferred HK$5 million into Kwong Kau’s personal bank account and gave him HK$450,000 as “tea money”. He also paid about HK$60,000 to the law firm handling the paperwork for the repayment, the court heard.
According to the elder Tam, Kwong Kau sought a HK$400,000 loan from him in December 2022, saying his bank account had been frozen by the commercial crime bureau because officers deemed the HK$5 million transfer suspicious.
Tam said he only gave his counterpart HK$250,000.
“Abby told me this person was not trustworthy, but because he had helped me settle this matter, I decided to help him,” the witness said, referring to the harassment by debt collectors.
The elder Tam said Kwong Kau never repaid him, but he had no intention of chasing the money because he did not think the retiree would pay it back.
Kwong Kau’s legal counsel, Oliver Davies, suggested that the elder Tam offered to lend his client money after the ex-sergeant said he was concerned that authorities would freeze his bank account.
“Ridiculous,” the witness replied.
The elder Tam said that after Choi’s killing came to light in February 2023, a law firm clerk sent him a photo of what appeared to be a handwritten letter from Kwong Kau, who asked him to hire lawyers on his behalf because he had been denied bail.
The defendant allegedly called himself a man with integrity, while describing the elder Tam as a “very good friend”, as he explained he was in a difficult situation because he had no money to hire legal representation.
“At that time I had a friend who was a lawyer and I consulted that person. I was advised to ignore him and that’s what I did,” the witness said.
The trial continues.

data.title: Private healthcare providers face new measures to make fees more transparent
data.description:
Private healthcare providers in Hong Kong will have to make their charges more transparent under government measures to be introduced from August next year at the earliest, including requirements to publish bilingual fee schedules and annual billing statistics.
The Health Bureau set out details of the proposed requirements for private hospitals and clinics in a document submitted to the Legislative Council on Thursday evening. The proposal was first floated in May last year.
The measures will cover price information, budget estimates and billing statistics.
“The government will introduce the regulation into the Legco by the end of the year and draw up the codes of practice, with a view to implementing the regulatory measures in phases starting from the second half of next year in an orderly manner,” the bureau said.
According to the timeline, the measures will apply to private hospitals from August next year at the earliest, followed by day procedure centres from November 2027 and clinics in mid-2028.
Under the proposals, all 14 private hospitals in the city, along with day procedure centres and clinics, will have to provide fee schedules in Chinese and English in a specified format. The schedules must describe all chargeable items and services and give either a fixed price or a price range for each.
The items will be grouped into 15 specified categories for private hospitals and 14 for day procedure centres and clinics.
Each facility must also clearly state whether additional charges apply for wards, operating theatres, medical procedure rooms or doctors’ services.
If a price cannot be provided in advance, for example, because it depends on a patient’s condition, the facility must state that the information will be provided separately.

All facilities must make their fee schedules available in printed or electronic form at all reception and cashier counters. Private hospitals must also make them available at admission offices and nursing stations, and on their websites.
Facilities must publish revised fee schedules and notify the Department of Health at least seven days before any price changes take effect.
All private hospitals will also have to provide patients with budget estimates in a specified format before admission, unless booking confirmation is issued no more than 12 hours beforehand. In such cases, hospitals will have to explain to patients why they cannot provide an estimate.
The estimates must cover both hospital and doctors’ fees.
If the final bill exceeds the estimate by 20 per cent or more, the hospital must provide the patient with a written explanation, a requirement the government had previously outlined.
“The purpose of setting the 20 per cent threshold is to ensure that patients are provided with an explanation when the final bill is significantly higher than the budget estimate, while avoiding the need for hospitals to provide explanations for ordinary charge variations,” the bureau said.
Private hospitals must also publish annual statistics on their fees and charges on their websites and submit them to the government.
Statistics on patients in standard beds who undergo a single treatment or procedure must be submitted to the government platform and published on hospital websites by March 31 each year. The figures must cover the previous calendar year.
“This requirement aims to ensure consistency in the data concerned in terms of the scope of treatments and procedures and ward class, thereby enhancing the comparability of statistics across different hospitals,” the bureau said.
Data submitted by private hospitals must be audited by a certified public accountant. If the audit cannot be completed in time, hospitals may submit and publish unaudited statistics by March 31.

data.title: Meet Nathan Chen, the Chinese teen AI prodigy courted by Silicon Valley
data.description:
A 17-year-old artificial intelligence researcher formerly with Moonshot AI has announced his departure for the United States, sparking intense speculation about his next move amid heated competition for elite talent between Silicon Valley and China’s tech hubs.
Nathan Chen Guangyu wrote on social media on Thursday that he had left the Beijing-based start-up after less than a year, describing his time there as “the best [year] of my life so far”.
The announcement caught many industry observers by surprise, given Chen’s brief tenure and the timing – coming just months ahead of Moonshot’s anticipated initial public offering in Hong Kong.
It also follows a string of successful releases by the start-up, including its latest flagship K3 model in July. The release sparked concern in Washington that the capability gap between US and Chinese frontier AI models had narrowed to its closest point yet.
Despite his short stint, Chen played an instrumental role in several of Moonshot’s core technical innovations in the past year, which helped make its Kimi models some of the world’s leading open-weight systems.

Among his contributions was a breakthrough technique known as “attention residuals”, which improves cost-efficiency and memory in Moonshot’s large language models. The method drew praise from high-profile industry figures, including OpenAI co-founders Andrej Karpathy and Elon Musk.
Speculation regarding Chen’s next job mounted after prominent figures from US start-ups, including Anthropic and Prime Intellect, commented on his post, congratulating him and inviting him to visit the San Francisco Bay Area.
One comment by Anthropic researcher Sholto Douglas suggested the two had recently met in person, sparking online rumours that Chen might join the Claude model developer.
However, in a follow-up post on X on Friday, Chen denied he was joining the US company, responding to a user’s question with a simple “No”.
As AI grows in geopolitical and commercial importance, young talent has become a hot commodity in China. Several key figures driving AI development at Chinese tech giants are Gen Z or millennials, including Tencent Holdings’ Vinces Yao Shunyu and Moonshot AI co-founder Yang Zhilin.
Chen is not the first teenage AI prodigy from China to make headlines. Former DeepSeek researcher Tu Jinhao gained prominence last year after co-authoring the Hangzhou-based start-up’s breakthrough R1 model paper while still a high school student in Shanghai.
Tu left DeepSeek to begin undergraduate studies at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.
Before joining Moonshot, Chen interned at a Silicon Valley start-up and was named a Rhodes Trust Rise Fellow – a global talent programme for young people aged 15 to 17 funded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and his wife, Wendy Schmidt.
Chen’s departure comes at a sensitive time. Last month, Beijing codified new restrictions barring top tech talent from leaving the country if their move would violate export controls or technology transfer regulations.

data.title: Beijing enlists multiple regulators to probe EV safety issue
data.description:
Beijing has enlisted the support of its top internet watchdog to deepen the investigation into a car safety issue that put Chinese-made intelligent vehicles under the spotlight.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Thursday that a joint investigation team including officials from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) would verify facts regarding reports about brake pedal failures in tests of an electric vehicle (EV) made by the Huawei Technologies-backed Maextro luxury brand.
The three ministry-level authorities “have paid close attention to the issue”, the MIIT said. “Relevant information will be released in a timely manner.”
The statement showed that Chinese authorities would be resolute in addressing concerns about Chinese EV quality and reliability amid a falling domestic market, analysts said.
On October 8, ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi released a video showing that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 multipurpose vehicles used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h.
The video went viral, while Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said in a commentary on Sunday that the incident underscored the importance of strengthened oversight over the country’s “rapidly developed” EVs.
“The internet regulator will be responsible for sifting out misinformation [about the matter] online that could taint the reputation of Chinese carmakers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “Consumers will be eager to see the truth amid regulators’ heightened investigation efforts.”
Maextro, jointly developed by Huawei and JAC and based in eastern China’s Anhui province, said in a statement on Thursday that it would fully cooperate with the investigation team to safeguard the interests of consumers and support the development of China’s EV industry.


On Sunday, the brand said that it would address the brake pedal issue by the end of this month. JAC assembles Maextro vehicles. Tech giant Huawei, through its Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance, supplies technology for smart driving and digital cockpits to the EVs.
The Maextro V800 is one of the most expensive EV models in mainland China, with a base price of 766,000 yuan (US$113,582).
On Saturday, the MIIT, along with three other ministry-level departments, published draft rules stipulating that sufficient vetting measures including 30,000km (18,641 miles) of road testing should be completed before any new model was offered to consumers.
Car sales in China slumped 21.7 per cent year on year to 13.3 million units in the first nine months of 2026 due to narrowing government support such as smaller EV purchase subsidies and a resumption of consumption tax.
In August, MIIT vice-minister Xin Guobin said at a press briefing in Beijing that new auto products and technologies would be barred from entering the market unless they passed stricter approval procedures.
Beijing is also carrying out a nationwide inspection campaign assessing the quality of Chinese-made cars.

data.title: Hong Kong woman gets 3 months in psychiatric institution over seditious posters
data.description:
An elderly woman who pasted materials containing pro-independence slogans and Hong Kong’s colonial-era flag outside her flat has been sentenced to three months in a maximum-security psychiatric institution for displaying seditious publications.
West Kowloon Court ordered housewife Yang Chau-ki, 62, to undergo mandatory psychiatric treatment at the Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre on Friday.
She was charged with knowingly displaying publications with seditious intent under Hong Kong’s Article 23 national security law, to which she pleaded not guilty.
Principal Magistrate Don So Man-lung heard that Yang, who was not represented by a lawyer, put up materials with seditious intent outside her flat at Tin Chung Court in Tin Shui Wai between March and November 2024.
The materials included a printout of Hong Kong’s colonial-era flag and prints with slogans from the 2019 anti-government protests, calling for the liberation of Hong Kong and her building.
She also displayed a fai chun, a traditional Chinese New Year decoration featuring poetic couplets, that referenced a revolutionary slogan.
So said that from the combined meaning of the slogans, it was “very clear” that Yang was dissatisfied with the current administration.
“The defendant intended to incite like-minded people to persist in their demands, carry out a revolution, overthrow the national government and restore British rule to Hong Kong,” he ruled. “This interpretation must be the only factual interpretation; there is no other.”
While So said he was satisfied with the defendant’s explanation that she was displeased with the security guard of her estate, he noted that pasting the publications “went way beyond that.”
“She had intentionally displayed the items and was well aware of the meaning of the slogans.”
So said that the slogans also did not display any suggestions for improvement for the current administration.
“Her intention was not to improve but to encourage the overthrow of the entire system and its replacement by the colonial-era system,” he said.
So ruled that Yang deliberately put up the items – which he described as “large and colourful” – on her door and in the public corridor for neighbours and other residents to see.
The posters included the words “Look but do not touch” and “Tear this down and your whole family will die,” which So said were warnings intended for her neighbours and the building management, as she knew they would attract attention.
He concluded that the defendant, knowing that the items and words were seditious, still posted them on the exterior of the flat with the intent of displaying them to neighbours and management staff.
“She wanted to incite their dissatisfaction with the current system, sow discord and prompt them to overthrow the government and restore British rule,” he said.
A psychiatric report previously obtained by the court indicated that Yang showed potential symptoms of schizophrenia and delusional disorder, though she was deemed fit to stand trial.

data.title: Hong Kong aims for share of HK$350 billion yacht industry as travel scheme opens
data.description:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched the Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme, with the transport minister announcing new measures to attract overseas captains.
The scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest policy address.
Under the scheme, mainland Chinese vessels can register through the Marine Department’s Electronic Business System to sail in Hong Kong waters.
Speaking at the launch ceremony, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the global yacht market was expected to reach HK$350 billion by 2032 and that Hong Kong was capable of obtaining a slice of the market.
He noted that there were around 6,000 superyachts in the world exceeding 30 metres (98.4 feet). More than 90 of them were in Hong Kong and the government planned to roll out more measures to boost the yacht economy.
“The outline of the national 15th five-year plan clearly calls for developing leisure consumption such as cruises and yachts, and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan also stated that we will actively develop it,” he said.
“Our vision for the yacht economy also reflects the global trend.”

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also said on Friday that the Marine Department would coordinate with local training institutions to offer online courses for overseas captains to turn the city into a hub for super yachts.
Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat said on Thursday that 23 individuals or groups had registered under the new travel scheme as of this week.
Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind Lantau Yacht Club, welcomed the “long-anticipated” scheme, saying the club had prepared for more mainland yachts coming to Hong Kong since 2019.
“We have special rates for our berths, and we purposely reserve space for people who come in on a transient basis, so we can accommodate yachts, unlike other yacht clubs that usually sell all that space to long-term owners,” he said.
Apart from berthing, the club also offers both long- and short-term service package discounts, including hotel accommodation and golf sessions, which are more cost-effective than a long-term membership.
Mak also noted that 10 mainland yachts have registered for the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show early next month and will start arriving from next week. They represented the largest number in years, up from just two to three previously.
Speaking on a radio programme, lawmaker Roy Chu Lap-wai described the registration of five yachts on the first day as “encouraging”.
“In the initial stage, I believe the five yachts that come here will go back and spread the word about how convenient and good Hong Kong is, if everything goes smoothly,” he said.
“More yacht owners who have been taking a wait-and-see approach may then be more proactive about applying. So I think it’s quite good.”
Chu said Hong Kong’s water supply and charging facilities were sufficient to meet demand at this stage, but more facilities and yacht clubs would be needed in the longer term to make the most of the scheme and boost the yacht economy.
Five designated berthing areas at Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung will provide 115 berths, in addition to those at private yacht clubs.

There are also seven kiosks supplying water to vessels and eight designated bunkering areas, according to the Water Supplies Department and the Marine Department.
Chu said Hong Kong had many distinctive islands for visiting yachts to explore. He hoped tourists would go island-hopping during the day, then dine and shop in urban areas at night.
“The government also held many successful big events, and they could get more involved in different aspects, so these relatively high-end, big-spending yacht tourists can really spend more money in Hong Kong and contribute to our economy,” he said.
Chu said the city could also develop a “one-day tour” and other services, such as chauffeur-driven cars with professional guides, adding that the Hong Kong Tourism Board could do more to promote these offerings and increase the economic benefits.

data.title: Beyond legal advice: Hong Kong charity helps bridge the gap in access to justice
data.description:
Pro Bono HK is known for helping people in need access justice in Hong Kong, but its work extends beyond legal advice to connecting clients with social workers and community groups for further support and promoting legal education.
Founded in 2014, the organisation helps people who may not qualify for legal aid or cannot afford private representation. Its work ranges from tenancy and family disputes to inheritance matters and emergency legal support.
Pro Bono HK and its volunteers are finalists for the Spirit of Teamwork Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.
CEO Vincent Yeung said founder Davyd Wong established the organisation to improve access to justice for people unable to obtain help through either private legal services or Hong Kong’s legal aid system.
“There are many people who require legal support but may not qualify for legal aid,” Yeung said. “That is the gap we are trying to address.”
Much of the organisation’s community work focuses on everyday problems facing lower-income households, including tenancy issues affecting subdivided-flat residents. It also works with NGOs to help frontline workers and residents understand legal rights.
Cases are screened before they reach a lawyer. Law students and interns handle initial inquiries, collect basic information and direct people to existing resources when legal advice is not needed.
“Sometimes all that the client needs is to be pointed in the right direction or given access to the right information,” Yeung said. “If more support is needed, we pair the client with a volunteer who has the right expertise and availability.”
Legal problems rarely arise in isolation, according to Victoria Wong Yin, a consultant supporting Pro Bono HK. Clients may also face housing, family or welfare difficulties, so the organisation works closely with registered social workers to identify those who need further support.
“There are two sides to it,” she said. “Clients need legal support, while social workers also need some basic legal knowledge to identify when professional legal advice is needed.”

The human side of legal advice is equally important, Yeung said. People seeking help may already be frightened or overwhelmed, particularly after a traumatic event.
“It is like a doctor’s bedside manner. How you explain the case matters,” she said.
After the deadly blaze at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November, Pro Bono HK and its volunteers produced bilingual legal information within 48 hours. They also mobilised hundreds of legal professionals to support affected residents through clinics, seminars and community outreach.
Yeung said some legal questions emerged only after the immediate emergency had passed.
“After a month or two, some affected residents began thinking about the legal issues,” he said, citing questions around property ownership, insurance and longer-term housing arrangements.
Pro Bono HK also wants to expand legal education to help people before problems develop into disputes.
Wong said such education should begin with young people, helping them understand the basics of contracts and scams, as well as the consequences of signing documents or allowing others to use their bank accounts.
“Education is very important because many people do not know what rights they have or what options are available to them,” she said.
Since January 2026, the organisation’s volunteers have contributed more than 1,500 hours of pro bono legal work, with about 70 lawyers and 30 students taking part, according to Yeung.
The organisation is considering expanding its work with schools. It also aims to make pro bono service a more regular part of legal practice through continued collaboration with social workers and community groups.
Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

data.title: Exclusive|Alo Yoga rakes in record HK$20 million in first-week sales at Hong Kong mall
data.description:
American athleisure brand Alo Yoga generated nearly HK$20 million (US$2.6 million) in sales during its first week in Hong Kong, breaking an opening-week record at a luxury waterfront shopping centre and highlighting growing appetite for premium wellness products amid an uneven retail recovery.
The brand, which soft opened its first Greater China flagship at K11 Musea in Tsim Sha Tsui on September 25, recorded the highest first-week sales among new stores at the mall, excluding jewellery and watch retailers.
The store is set to hold its official grand opening on Friday evening.
The nearly HK$20 million haul came from its two-storey, 7,000 square foot flagship, which occupies the former premises of British luxury food retailer Fortnum & Mason. The British brand closed its Hong Kong outlet in January.
Horace Lam, CEO of K11 Hong Kong, attributed the strong debut to the brand’s celebrity appeal, pent-up consumer demand and its ability to combine luxury fashion with wellness.
“I think it has created the luxury wellness category,” Lam told the South China Morning Post, adding that traditional sportswear and luxury brands had rarely sought to combine the two concepts so deliberately.

The brand’s strategy extended from product design and pricing to marketing and the in-store experience, setting it apart from more established competitors, he said.
Lam said Alo’s opening was deliberately timed ahead of the National Day “golden week” holiday to capitalise on an influx of mainland Chinese tourists.
Tourists accounted for about 60 per cent of the store’s sales, while local customers contributed the remaining 40 per cent, according to K11 Musea.
The strong debut coincided with a rebound in inbound tourism. Hong Kong welcomed 4.03 million visitors in September, up 22 per cent year on year, according to figures released by the Tourism Board on Thursday.
Mainland arrivals jumped 29 per cent to about 3.17 million, while total visitor numbers in the first nine months reached 40.7 million, an increase of 12 per cent.
Lam said maintaining a healthy balance between local and tourist spending had become increasingly important for Hong Kong retailers, helping businesses avoid excessive reliance on peak holiday periods.
He also credited Alo’s popularity to its community-focused marketing strategy, which included exclusive yoga, running and cycling activities ahead of the opening.
The brand, endorsed by celebrities including Blackpink’s Jisoo and Kendall Jenner, had accumulated substantial demand in Greater China before establishing physical stores in the region, he said.
Its celebrity appeal will be on display at Friday’s official opening, which Jisoo is expected to attend.
Jackie Wong, director of occupier services at Colliers, said changing consumer preferences were driving demand for larger retail spaces among wellness and lifestyle brands.
“Consumers are increasingly looking beyond the product itself and placing greater value on experiences, lifestyle, wellness and well-being,” she said.
“For wellness and active-lifestyle brands in particular, a larger retail footprint makes strategic sense as the store is a part of the brand experience and brand positioning.”
Wong said softer rents were also creating opportunities for retailers to secure prominent locations at more affordable costs, even as the leasing market showed signs of recovery.

High-street rents rose 1.8 per cent in the first nine months of the year, according to Colliers, which forecast growth of about 3 per cent for 2026.
“Brands are therefore becoming more selective rather than simply more aggressive,” she said, adding that retailers were prioritising prime locations offering strong visibility and footfall at viable occupancy costs.
Growing demand from personal care, lifestyle and other experience-led operators also reflected the continuing evolution of Hong Kong’s retail mix, she added.
Lam said the mall had been adjusting its tenant mix in response to changing shopping habits, with the arrival of Alo forming part of a broader strategy to introduce more lifestyle-oriented brands.
K11 Musea, which also recently welcomed Prada, Miu Miu and Max Mara, said that in the past financial year it had recorded its highest annual sales since opening.
Most of its current luxury-brand upgrades are expected to be completed by Christmas, with further changes planned for the upper and basement floors in 2027 and 2028.
Alo, meanwhile, plans to open nine stores across Hong Kong, Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Chengdu and Macau as part of its Greater China expansion.

data.title: HSBC to double Hong Kong AI team to 300, outpacing Singapore plan
data.description:
HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, said on Thursday it would double its artificial intelligence specialist team in the city to 300, a figure much larger than the workforce planned for its recently announced AI centre in Singapore.
The announcement comes after Hong Kong’s regulators were reported to have raised concerns about the Singapore hub.
The bank would double its AI specialist headcount in Hong Kong from 150 to 300 over the next two to three years, said David Liao Yi-chien, HSBC co-CEO for Asia and the Middle East, in a media briefing after attending an industry event hosted by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).
HSBC would also launch the Hong Kong AI Institute next year, he said.
“Hong Kong is our home market at HSBC. We are using Hong Kong as the hub to develop our digital finance and embrace new technologies to better serve customers and support Hong Kong’s digital ambitions and growth,” Liao said.
Four members of the bank’s 13-member group operating committee were based in Hong Kong, underscoring the city’s importance to HSBC, he added.
The remarks marked the lender’s first public comments since it announced plans in late July to set up a Singapore AI centre and hire 100 specialists.
A source told the South China Morning Post last week that the HKMA had privately questioned HSBC about the decision.
Liao did not confirm the conversation with the HKMA, but said: “HSBC always has positive dialogues with the regulator.”
He said HSBC, as an international bank, “will always invest in AI in different markets, including mainland China, the UK and the Middle East, but Hong Kong will always be the core part of that investment”.
Hong Kong’s five-year plan, with AI as a pillar of development, “will give us a lot of opportunities”, Liao said. “HSBC has spent over [US$14 billion] on a buyout of shares from subsidiary Hang Seng Bank in January, which represents an important investment in Hong Kong.”
Liao spoke on the same day that the HKMA hosted an AI summit and highlighted use cases for the technology in Hong Kong’s finance sector.
Hong Kong’s development plan, with AI investment and development identified as a priority, could intensify competition with Singapore, analysts said.

The HKMA said on Thursday that 20 banks and 14 technology companies had completed sandbox testing of 27 AI use cases. HSBC alone contributed two use cases, including a language-to-sign-language translator for customers with hearing difficulties, and the use of AI to detect deepfakes during account opening.
The de facto central bank also announced new principles for banks’ use of AI, built around what it called the ART framework, which stood for accountability, resilience and trust. Under the principles, which took effect on Thursday, banks must appoint a responsible person for each AI application and maintain records of AI use cases and the associated risk-management measures.
In the coming weeks, the HKMA would also introduce a discussion paper on the governance of agentic AI and launch a platform for sharing AI training data, it said.
HKMA deputy CEO Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang said the discussion paper would focus on ensuring agentic AI systems operated according to their intended purpose and did not become “rogue agents”.
Banks would need a “kill switch” to stop agentic AI systems if they malfunctioned, while also maintaining fallback arrangements that allow human intervention to take over tasks when necessary, Yuen said, adding that the approach was aligned with international practices.
“The progression from generative to agentic AI represents an important new stage of innovation for the banking sector,” Yuen said.
Under Fintech 2030, the HKMA has encouraged banks to embrace AI, although such development must be supported by effective risk management and governance, he added.
“By pairing innovation with clear accountability, resilient operating models and effective human oversight, banks can fully realise the benefits of AI while maintaining the trust and stability of Hong Kong’s financial system,” Yuen said.

data.title: Lidar maker Hesai launches 3D spatial camera with ambitions to train robotsThe launch marks the latest step in the firm’s push to broaden its business beyond vehicles and establish a foothold in the e
data.description:
Hesai Group, the world’s largest maker of lidar sensors for vehicles, has launched a 3D spatial camera as it expands into physical artificial intelligence in search of new growth opportunities.
The handheld device, called Kosmo, is described by Hesai as a “physical AI eye” and converts real-world environments into detailed, editable 3D models. The company said it was designed to standardise the digitisation of complex spaces such as campuses and factories.
“Our interesting new products, which represent an extension of our innovative capabilities, will lead to some new business patterns,” David Li Yifan, CEO of Hesai, told reporters in a media briefing on Wednesday.
“Hesai has some other product series in the pipeline that can contribute to the development of the infrastructure for the entire physical AI industry.”
Kosmo is supported by an intelligent platform that integrates AI algorithms, digital 3D models and cloud services. The company said the device could help filmmakers, video game developers and cultural service providers convert physical environments into production-ready 3D content more quickly.
Li said Hesai envisioned building a Kosmo platform to help train robots as embodied AI develops. The company has partnered with Pixar Animation Studios to develop Kosmo-related technologies.
The CEO said Hesai aimed to evolve into a broader technology company as the AI industry grows, adding that its technologies and products could eventually be supplied to businesses such as humanoid robot makers.


In August, Andrew Fan, chief financial officer of the Shanghai-based firm, told the South China Morning Post that the company was more than an automotive supplier, pointing to its push into AI-related products.
In April, Hesai unveiled its “6D” full-colour platform, saying it would enable lidar sensors to measure distances and identify small objects with industry-leading performance. It describes the technology as 6D because of the sensors’ ability to detect the X, Y and Z coordinates of an object, plus its reflectivity, velocity and colour.
The lidar sensors are powered by Hesai’s self-developed Picasso chip and have not yet been delivered to customers.
Hesai’s push into AI comes as Beijing seeks to make China a global leader in robotics, backed by a strong supply chain for the industry.
China is already the world’s largest market for industrial robots and a leading developer of humanoids. In 2024, it accounted for 54 per cent of the world’s industrial robot installations, ­according to data released by the International Federation of Robotics in September 2025.
Hesai’s lidar sensors help intelligent vehicles map their surroundings. The company supplies products to China’s 10 largest automotive groups.
The company reported net income of 70.6 million yuan (US$10.4 million) for the three months ended June, up 60 per cent from a year earlier. Revenue grew 21 per cent to 860.8 million yuan, it said.

data.title: HSBC launches discretionary portfolio management service for retail investors
data.description:
HSBC has launched a discretionary portfolio management service for retail investors with a minimum investment threshold as low as HK$1,000 (US$128) per month, as Hong Kong’s largest lender aims to attract younger, tech-savvy customers.
The new service, “Portfolio+”, allows HSBC’s retail banking customers in Hong Kong to build a discretionary investment portfolio via the company’s mobile apps with a lump sum of at least HK$10,000 or regular contributions of HK$1,000 per month, according to Winnie Ng, head of wealth and Premier solutions at HSBC Hong Kong.
Investors could choose to allocate their investments at different risk levels or under themes such as green concepts, with the bank then investing the funds and rebalancing the investment mix according to its house view, Ng told reporters ahead of the service’s launch on Thursday.
“We would like to capture the young investors aged 35 or younger who are too busy to invest or who have little or no investment experience. Our investment experts can invest for them according to their risk appetite and investment goals,” she said.
“With the help of technology to do analysis and documentation work, we can now introduce the discretionary investment services to the mass market of retail investors. Previously, we could only provide such a type of service to private bank clients as discretionary services involve a lot of manual work.”

HSBC Hong Kong has 7 million customers – a figure almost equal to the city’s population – and the bank has focused on promoting its investment and wealth management business in the city in recent years.
The discretionary investment service will charge a fee of 0.5 to 0.8 per cent per annum, based on the portfolio’s assets under management, charged monthly, according to the bank.
Allen Chiu, head of discretionary and funds specialists at HSBC Hong Kong wealth and premier solutions, said Portfolio+ would adopt a globally diversified approach, investing in stocks and bonds in the United States, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region and emerging economies.
The lower-risk portfolios were more heavily weighted towards global fixed income, while higher-risk portfolios had greater equity exposure, particularly to US markets, he said.
“Diversification would be the key of success for investors to cope with the volatile markets and achieve growth of their investment for the long term,” Chiu said.
Ng said the bank would invest these assets via exchange-traded funds listed in London, while it would consider investing in Hong Kong ETFs in the next stage. The portfolios also include selective alternative-asset-style exposure, such as listed property and infrastructure ETFs.

data.title: Hong Kong vies for role in robot boom with embodied AI hub launch
data.description:
The Hong Kong Productivity Council (HKPC) opened the city’s first experimental hub for embodied artificial intelligence on Thursday with the participation of seven mainland and Hong Kong companies, including industry leaders Unitree Robotics and Galbot, as the city looks to carve out a role in the global robotics boom.
Located at the HKPC Building in Kowloon Tong, the Embodied AI International Applications Hub, housed under the HKPC’s industrial AI and robotics centre, features simulated real-world environments where the companies can test and optimise their latest robotic designs, ahead of potential global roll-outs.
“Hong Kong’s application scenarios have an international characteristic,” said Sunny Tan, HKPC chairman, at the opening ceremony. “For many mainland robot manufacturers, they can train their robots for international application scenarios without leaving the country here.”
Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong said that the hub marked a major milestone in Hong Kong’s efforts to align with national initiatives to advance in embodied AI and robotics, and pledged further government support to promote development in the field.
“Humanoid robotics and embodied AI are key frontiers of the next wave of technological innovation, with tremendous potential to transform industrial operations and foster new quality productive forces,” he said.
Hong Kong’s unique advantage lies in its international demand and its pool of global talent
Jason Chen, Galbot
The hub will initially feature a cohort of seven technology partners and eight “scenario partners” – government bodies and major enterprises that will deploy the latest robots in various application settings. These include Hong Kong’s Civil Engineering and Development Department and electronics company TCL.
Edmond Lai, HKPC’s chief digital officer, said that the partnerships would address one of the main bottlenecks for the robotics industry: a lack of real-world testing environments.
“Different regions are still at the stage of formulating standards for embodied AI, and this is a golden window period,” he said.
“Through this training hub, we hope to establish these practices so they can be pushed forward as potential industry standards.”
Following the ceremony, industry leaders and media were guided through live demonstrations from the seven robotics companies.
Tsinghua University-backed Robotera showcased its M7 humanoid robot, which has already been deployed in facilities of SF Express and China Post, while domestic humanoid robot leader Unitree showcased its R1 humanoid and A2 quadruped robots, which can be used for factory inspections.

Meanwhile, Shenzhen’s AI Squared Robotics and Beijing’s Galbot both showcased use of their robots in retail settings, including the preparing and retrieving of beverages.
The sole local firm was Hong Kong start-up Rice Robotics, which showcased its NEX semi-humanoid robot, designed for smart libraries and educational environments.
Jason Chen, senior vice-president at Galbot, said that he hoped the partnership with HKPC, and his company’s recent opening of three fully autonomous robot-staffed retail stores in the city, would popularise robots among the public.
“Hong Kong’s unique advantage lies in its international demand and its pool of global talent,” he told the South China Morning Post.

data.title: More than music: Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra strikes a chord across generations
data.description:
For nearly five decades, the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra has worked to bring its music to a wider audience, including people who might never have considered entering a concert hall.
Executive director Celina Chin Man-wah said the orchestra had long sought to ensure Chinese music was not seen as distant, formal or difficult to understand.
That has meant commissioning new works, exploring different musical styles and developing programmes for younger audiences.
“We cannot rely on the old repertoire alone,” Chin said. “New works are essential if Chinese music is to keep developing and speak to future audiences.”
The orchestra has commissioned more than 2,400 works over the years, and its musicians have collaborated with composers and artists from Hong Kong, mainland China and around the world.
Its international engagements have also helped bring Chinese orchestral music to wider audiences.
Chin recalled an invitation to perform as part of the opening programme at Beijing’s National Centre for the Performing Arts, adding that overseas presenters had also requested programmes of contemporary Chinese music.
She also said such invitations recognised not only the orchestra’s performances but also its role in creating and promoting new repertoire.

Chin joined the orchestra in 1996 after holding arts management roles in theatre, film festivals and arts programming. Those roles gave her experience in production, logistics and programming that she would draw on at the orchestra.
The orchestra is a finalist for the Spirit of Culture Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.
Its work extends beyond the concert hall. Chin sees Chinese music as a way to bring communities together, encouraging people of different ages and backgrounds to take part.
The orchestra launched its Hong Kong Drum Festival in 2003 after the Sars outbreak, partly to help lift morale. Participants have since included children, parents, older people and members of rehabilitation organisations.
The orchestra has also worked with young people in correctional institutions. Chin recalled programmes in which participants learned percussion and performed for their families, culminating in a piece they played together with their relatives.
The aim, she said, went beyond music.
“Sometimes a young person has an idea and the family may not understand it, or the family has expectations the young person cannot accept,” she said. “To complete the piece, they have to listen to each other and work together.”
Chin advocates introducing children to music at an early age, whether or not they go on to become professional musicians.

She also sees a growing range of career opportunities in the arts. Young performers may later move into teaching, composition, music therapy or other creative fields, while some independent artists develop their own projects and build careers outside traditional institutions.
The orchestra also gives younger composers opportunities to have their new works performed by professional musicians, allowing them to hear how their compositions work in practice and exchange ideas directly with the players.
Chin said such programmes could not always be judged by immediate audience numbers or ticket revenue.
“Art cannot always be assessed by whether something is popular straight away,” she said. “Artistic development takes patience, and audiences need time to discover work with greater depth.”
Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.
